claim: A high-fat diet (HFD) in mice causes early loss of expression of the glycolytic enzyme Hexokinase 2 (HK2) specifically in adipose tissue.
source: Here, we show that a high-fat diet (HFD) in mice causes early loss of expression of the glycolytic enzyme Hexokinase 2 (HK2) specifically in adipose tissue.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from proteomic analysis and immunoblotting showing HK2 downregulation in adipose tissue of HFD-fed mice.

claim: Adipose-specific knockout of Hk2 reduced glucose disposal and lipogenesis in adipose tissue.
source: Adipose-specific knockout of Hk2 reduced glucose disposal and lipogenesis and enhanced fatty acid release in adipose tissue.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from AdHk2KO mice showing reduced glucose uptake and lipogenesis.

claim: Adipose-specific knockout of Hk2 enhanced fatty acid release in adipose tissue.
source: Adipose-specific knockout of Hk2 reduced glucose disposal and lipogenesis and enhanced fatty acid release in adipose tissue.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased NEFA release in AdHk2KO mice.

claim: Hk2 knockout promoted glucose production in liver in a non-cell-autonomous manner.
source: In a non-cell-autonomous manner, Hk2 knockout also promoted glucose production in liver.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp studies and pyruvate tolerance tests showing increased hepatic glucose production in AdHk2KO mice.

claim: Reduced hexokinase activity was observed in adipose tissue of obese and diabetic patients.
source: Furthermore, we observed reduced hexokinase activity in adipose tissue of obese and diabetic patients, and identified a loss-of-function mutation in the hk2 gene of naturally hyperglycemic Mexican cavefish.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from human omental WAT biopsies showing reduced hexokinase activity.

claim: A loss-of-function mutation in the hk2 gene was identified in naturally hyperglycemic Mexican cavefish.
source: Furthermore, we observed reduced hexokinase activity in adipose tissue of obese and diabetic patients, and identified a loss-of-function mutation in the hk2 gene of naturally hyperglycemic Mexican cavefish.
evidence: Supported by DNA sequencing data and functional assays showing the R42H mutation reduces HK2 activity.

claim: HFD in mice led to loss of HK2 by inhibiting translation of Hk2 mRNA.
source: Mechanistically, HFD in mice led to loss of HK2 by inhibiting translation of Hk2 mRNA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from AHA-incorporation assays showing reduced HK2 synthesis in vWAT of HFD-fed mice.

claim: Obesity-induced loss of adipose HK2 is an evolutionarily conserved mechanism for the development of selective insulin resistance and hyperglycemia.
source: Our findings identify adipose HK2 as a critical mediator of local and systemic glucose homeostasis, and suggest that obesity-induced loss of adipose HK2 is an evolutionarily conserved mechanism for the development of selective insulin resistance and thereby hyperglycemia.
evidence: Based on inference from findings in mice, humans, and cavefish showing similar patterns of HK2 loss associated with hyperglycemia.

claim: Adipose tissue plays a particularly important role in systemic glucose homeostasis despite its minor contribution to glucose clearance.
source: Although its contribution to glucose clearance is minor (Jackson et al., 1986; Kowalski and Bruce, 2014), adipose tissue plays a particularly important role in systemic glucose homeostasis (Abel et al., 2001; Shepherd et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Adipose-specific knockout of insulin signaling components results in local and systemic insulin insensitivity.
source: Adipose-specific knockout of insulin signaling components, such as the insulin receptor, mTORC2, and AKT, results in local and systemic insulin insensitivity (Beg et al., 2017; Cybulski et al., 2009; Frei et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2003; Kumar et al., 2010; Sakaguchi et al., 2017; Shearin et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Diet-induced obesity in mice causes adipose dysfunction, systemic insulin insensitivity, and hyperglycemia despite normal insulin signaling in white adipose tissue.
source: However, we and others have reported that diet-induced obesity in mice causes adipose dysfunction, systemic insulin insensitivity, and hyperglycemia despite normal insulin signaling in white adipose tissue (WAT; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Shimobayashi et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to published literature, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HK2 is the most abundant (~80%) of the three hexokinase isoforms expressed in vWAT.
source: HK2 is the most abundant (~80%) of the three hexokinase isoforms expressed in vWAT but the only one down-regulated upon HFD (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HK2 is the only hexokinase isoform down-regulated upon HFD in vWAT.
source: HK2 is the most abundant (~80%) of the three hexokinase isoforms expressed in vWAT but the only one down-regulated upon HFD (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HK2 expression was reduced by approximately 60% in vWAT of 4 week HFD mice.
source: Quantification by immunoblotting revealed an approximately 60%, 90% and 50% reduction in HK2 expression in vWAT, subcutaneous WAT (sWAT), and brown adipose tissue (BAT), respectively, of 4 week HFD mice (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: HK2 expression was reduced by approximately 90% in sWAT of 4 week HFD mice.
source: Quantification by immunoblotting revealed an approximately 60%, 90% and 50% reduction in HK2 expression in vWAT, subcutaneous WAT (sWAT), and brown adipose tissue (BAT), respectively, of 4 week HFD mice (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: HK2 expression was reduced by approximately 50% in BAT of 4 week HFD mice.
source: Quantification by immunoblotting revealed an approximately 60%, 90% and 50% reduction in HK2 expression in vWAT, subcutaneous WAT (sWAT), and brown adipose tissue (BAT), respectively, of 4 week HFD mice (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Hexokinase activity was decreased in WAT of HFD-fed mice.
source: Consistent with reduced HK2 expression, hexokinase activity was decreased in WAT of HFD-fed mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by hexokinase activity assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: HK2 expression was decreased in WAT of ND-fed ob/ob mice compared to littermate controls.
source: HK2 expression was also decreased in WAT of ND-fed ob/ob mice, compared to littermate controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that loss of HK2 is common to different obesogenic conditions.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Loss of HK2 is common to different obesogenic conditions.
source: HK2 expression was also decreased in WAT of ND-fed ob/ob mice, compared to littermate controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that loss of HK2 is common to different obesogenic conditions.
evidence: Based on inference from observations in both HFD-fed and ob/ob mice.

claim: HK2 downregulation in adipose tissue occurred within one week of HFD and correlated with systemic insulin insensitivity.
source: A longitudinal study of HFD-fed mice revealed that HK2 down-regulation in adipose tissue occurred within one week of HFD and correlated with systemic insulin insensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: HK2 expression was unchanged in skeletal muscle of HFD-fed mice.
source: HK2 expression was unchanged in skeletal muscle (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of the glucose transporter GLUT4 was slightly reduced in vWAT at 4 weeks of HFD.
source: Expression of the glucose transporter GLUT4 was slightly reduced in vWAT at 4 weeks of HFD (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by proteomic and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: GLUT4 was down-regulated in sWAT at >1 week of HFD.
source: In sWAT, GLUT4 was down-regulated at >1 week of HFD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Insulin signaling was normal in WAT at 4 weeks of HFD.
source: Confirming earlier observations (Shimobayashi et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2015), insulin signaling was normal in WAT at 4 weeks of HFD (Figure 1—figure supplements 1A and 2D–E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data and citations to published literature.

claim: Insulin signaling was significantly downregulated in BAT within 1 week of HFD.
source: However, in BAT, insulin signaling was significantly downregulated within 1 week of HFD (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Shifting from HFD to 2 weeks of ND restored HK2 expression and normal blood glucose.
source: Shifting from HFD to 2 weeks of ND restored HK2 expression and normal blood glucose (Figure 1E–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and glucose measurement data shown in Figure 1E-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Loss of HK2 expression upon obesogenic conditions is an adipose-specific, transient physiological response that correlates with hyperglycemia.
source: Thus, loss of HK2 expression upon obesogenic conditions is an adipose-specific, transient physiological response that correlates with hyperglycemia.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations showing tissue-specific and reversible HK2 loss.

claim: Omental WAT biopsies from obese non-diabetic and obese diabetic patients displayed a ~30% reduction in hexokinase activity.
source: Similar to our findings in mice, omental WAT (human vWAT) biopsies from obese non-diabetic and obese diabetic patients displayed a~30% reduction in hexokinase activity (Figure 1G and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by hexokinase activity assay data from human samples shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Hexokinase activity was particularly low in obese non-diabetic patients with severe insulin resistance compared to patients with mild insulin resistance.
source: Importantly, hexokinase activity was particularly low in obese non-diabetic patients with severe insulin resistance, compared to patients with mild insulin resistance (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by hexokinase activity assay data from human samples shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Hexokinase activity negatively correlated with insulin resistance in obese patients, but this correlation was not statistically significant.
source: Although hexokinase activity negatively correlated with insulin resistance in obese patients, this correlation was not statistically significant (Figure 1I), suggesting that loss of hexokinase activity may not be the only cause of insulin resistance in human.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Loss of hexokinase activity may not be the only cause of insulin resistance in humans.
source: Although hexokinase activity negatively correlated with insulin resistance in obese patients, this correlation was not statistically significant (Figure 1I), suggesting that loss of hexokinase activity may not be the only cause of insulin resistance in human.
evidence: Based on inference from non-significant correlation data.

claim: Ducluzeau et al. observed a decrease in HK2 mRNA expression in adipose tissue of diabetic patients.
source: We note that Ducluzeau et al. observed a decrease in HK2 mRNA expression in adipose tissue of diabetic patients (Ducluzeau et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: HK2 down-regulation in adipose tissue is a key event, possibly causal, in obesity-induced insulin insensitivity and hyperglycemia in mouse and human.
source: Altogether, the above findings suggest that HK2 down-regulation in adipose tissue is a key event, possibly causal, in obesity-induced insulin insensitivity and hyperglycemia in mouse and human.
evidence: Based on inference from combined findings in mice and humans.

claim: Mexican cavefish (Astyanax mexicanus) are hyperglycemic compared to surface fish from which they are descended.
source: Mexican cavefish (Astyanax mexicanus), also known as blind fish, are hyperglycemic compared to surface fish from which they are descended (Riddle et al., 2018; Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and reference to Figure 2A-B.

claim: Hyperglycemia is a selected trait in cavefish that presumably allows cave-dwelling fish to survive in nutrient-limited conditions.
source: Hyperglycemia, although a pathological condition in mouse and human, is a selected trait that presumably allows cave-dwelling fish to survive in nutrient-limited conditions.
evidence: Based on speculation about evolutionary adaptation.

claim: Pachón and Tinaja cavefish acquired a loss-of-function mutation in the insulin receptor gene, causing insulin resistance and hyperglycemia.
source: Among three independently evolved cavefish isolates, Pachón and Tinaja cavefish (names refer to the caves from which the fish were isolated) acquired a loss-of-function mutation in the insulin receptor gene, causing insulin resistance and hyperglycemia (Riddle et al., 2018; Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Molino cavefish is the most hyperglycemic but contains a wild-type insulin receptor gene and displays normal insulin signaling.
source: The third isolate, Molino cavefish, is the most hyperglycemic but contains a wild-type insulin receptor gene and displays normal insulin signaling (Riddle et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A homozygous, missense mutation in the coding region of the Molino hk2 gene changed highly conserved arginine 42 (R42) to histidine (R42H).
source: The homozygous, missense mutation in the coding region of the Molino hk2 gene changed highly conserved arginine 42 (R42) to histidine (R42H) (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: R42 forms a salt bridge with aspartic acid 272 (D272) to stabilize the conformation of HK2.
source: Based on the published structure of HK2 (Nawaz et al., 2018), R42 forms a salt bridge with aspartic acid 272 (D272) to stabilize the conformation of HK2 (Figure 2E), predicting that R42H destabilizes HK2 and is thus a loss-of-function mutation.
evidence: Based on structural analysis using published HK2 structure, shown in Figure 2E.

claim: R42H destabilizes HK2 and is thus a loss-of-function mutation.
source: Based on the published structure of HK2 (Nawaz et al., 2018), R42 forms a salt bridge with aspartic acid 272 (D272) to stabilize the conformation of HK2 (Figure 2E), predicting that R42H destabilizes HK2 and is thus a loss-of-function mutation.
evidence: Based on inference from structural analysis.

claim: Molino HK2 displayed little-to-no hexokinase activity compared to surface fish HK2 when expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: Indeed, Molino HK2 displayed little-to-no hexokinase activity compared to surface fish HK2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by hexokinase activity assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: HK2-R42H displayed ~50% hexokinase activity compared to HK2-WT in mammalian cells.
source: HK2-R42H displayed ~50% hexokinase activity compared to HK2-WT, despite similar expression levels (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by hexokinase activity assay data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The R42H mutation may account for the hyperglycemia in Molino cavefish.
source: Thus, the R42H mutation may account for the hyperglycemia in Molino cavefish.
evidence: Based on inference from functional data showing reduced HK2 activity.

claim: R42H in Molino appears to be a genetically fixed version of what is observed in mice as a physiological down-regulation of HK2 in response to HFD.
source: In other words, R42H in Molino appears to be a genetically fixed version of what we observe in mice as a physiological down-regulation of HK2 in response to HFD.
evidence: Based on inference comparing genetic and physiological mechanisms.

claim: The findings in Molino provide orthogonal evidence that the down-regulation of HK2 in mice is physiologically relevant in hyperglycemia.
source: Although further study is required to link the R42H mutation to the hyperglycemic phenotype in Molino cavefish, the findings in Molino provide orthogonal evidence that the down-regulation of HK2 in mice is physiologically relevant in hyperglycemia.
evidence: Based on inference from comparative findings across species.

claim: HK2-knockdown pre-adipocytes differentiated normally to produce mature adipocytes.
source: HK2-knockdown pre-adipocytes differentiated normally to produce mature adipocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by differentiation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The glycolytic rate was lower in HK2-knockdown adipocytes compared to controls.
source: The glycolytic rate was lower in HK2-knockdown adipocytes compared to controls, as measured by extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) (Figure 3C) and lactate production (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by ECAR and lactate production assay data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Insulin-stimulated glucose accumulation was 50% lower in HK2-knockdown adipocytes despite normal insulin signaling.
source: Furthermore, although basal glucose accumulation did not differ, insulin-stimulated glucose accumulation was 50% lower in HK2-knockdown adipocytes (Figure 3E), despite normal insulin signaling (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by glucose uptake assay and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3E and 3A.

claim: HK2-knockdown has no effect on basal glucose accumulation because HK2 is inactive in the absence of insulin.
source: The observation that HK2-knockdown has no effect on basal glucose accumulation is due to the fact that HK2 is inactive in the absence of insulin (Gottlob et al., 2001; Miyamoto et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of HK2 decreases glucose disposal in insulin-stimulated adipocytes in vitro.
source: Thus, loss of HK2 decreases glucose disposal in insulin-stimulated adipocytes in vitro.
evidence: Based on inference from in vitro experimental data.

claim: HK2 expression was decreased ~75% in vWAT of AdHk2KO mice.
source: In AdHk2KO mice, HK2 expression was decreased ~75% in vWAT,~70% in sWAT, and ~65% in BAT but unchanged in skeletal muscle (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: HK2 expression was decreased ~70% in sWAT of AdHk2KO mice.
source: In AdHk2KO mice, HK2 expression was decreased ~75% in vWAT,~70% in sWAT, and ~65% in BAT but unchanged in skeletal muscle (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: HK2 expression was decreased ~65% in BAT of AdHk2KO mice.
source: In AdHk2KO mice, HK2 expression was decreased ~75% in vWAT,~70% in sWAT, and ~65% in BAT but unchanged in skeletal muscle (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: HK2 expression was unchanged in skeletal muscle of AdHk2KO mice.
source: In AdHk2KO mice, HK2 expression was decreased ~75% in vWAT,~70% in sWAT, and ~65% in BAT but unchanged in skeletal muscle (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Glycolytic metabolites were decreased in WAT of AdHk2KO mice.
source: Glycolytic metabolites were also decreased in WAT (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Insulin signaling was normal in adipose tissue of AdHk2KO mice.
source: Furthermore, insulin signaling was normal in adipose tissue (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C) and other tissues (see below) of AdHk2KO mice.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: ND-fed AdHk2KO mice were insulin insensitive and severely glucose intolerant.
source: However, contrary to controls, ND-fed AdHk2KO mice were insulin insensitive and severely glucose intolerant as measured by conventional tolerance tests (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: Supported by ITT and GTT data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Glucose intolerance was observed in adipose-specific heterozygous Hk2 knockout mice.
source: Moreover, glucose intolerance was observed in adipose-specific heterozygous Hk2 knockout mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by GTT data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Partial loss of HK2, as observed in HFD-fed wild-type mice, is sufficient to cause glucose intolerance.
source: These data indicate that partial loss of HK2, as observed in HFD-fed wild-type mice (Figure 1), is sufficient to cause glucose intolerance.
evidence: Based on inference from heterozygous knockout data.

claim: AdHk2KO mice required significantly less or no infusion of glucose to maintain euglycemia during hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp compared to control mice.
source: Compared to control mice, AdHk2KO mice required significantly less or no infusion of glucose to maintain euglycemia (Figure 4E–F), despite similar hyperinsulinemia (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by clamp study data shown in Figure 4E-F and Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Loss of HK2 specifically in adipose tissue is sufficient to cause insulin insensitivity and hyperglycemia, even in ND-fed mice.
source: The above findings confirm that loss of HK2 specifically in adipose tissue is sufficient to cause insulin insensitivity and thereby hyperglycemia, even in ND-fed mice.
evidence: Based on inference from AdHk2KO mouse phenotype data.

claim: Reduced glucose uptake in adipose tissue was observed in AdHk2KO mice in vivo.
source: Consistent with reduced glucose accumulation observed in adipocytes in vitro (Figure 3E), we also observed reduced glucose uptake in adipose tissue in vivo, as measured upon injection of the glucose tracer 14C-2-deoxyglucose during our hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp studies (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by glucose uptake assay data from clamp studies shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Adipose tissue accounts for only <5% of glucose disposal.
source: However, adipose tissue accounts for only <5% of glucose disposal (Jackson et al., 1986; Kowalski and Bruce, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Glucose uptake in skeletal muscle was unimpaired in AdHk2KO mice.
source: Glucose uptake in skeletal muscle, which accounts for 70–80% of insulin-inducible glucose clearance (Kowalski and Bruce, 2014), was unimpaired in AdHk2KO mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by glucose uptake assay data shown in Figure 5A and citation to published literature.

claim: Skeletal muscle accounts for 70-80% of insulin-inducible glucose clearance.
source: Glucose uptake in skeletal muscle, which accounts for 70–80% of insulin-inducible glucose clearance (Kowalski and Bruce, 2014), was unimpaired in AdHk2KO mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Plasma insulin levels were similar in AdHk2KO and control mice.
source: Plasma insulin levels were also similar in AdHk2KO and control mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by insulin measurement data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Insulin signaling was not affected in skeletal muscle and liver of fasted and re-fed AdHk2KO mice.
source: Moreover, insulin signaling was not affected in skeletal muscle and liver of fasted and re-fed AdHk2KO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The severity of glucose intolerance in AdHk2KO mice is not due to defects in glucose uptake in skeletal muscle, insulin secretion or insulin signaling in peripheral tissues.
source: These findings indicate that the severity of the glucose intolerance in AdHk2KO mice is not due to defects in glucose uptake in skeletal muscle, insulin secretion or insulin signaling in peripheral tissues.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing normal muscle glucose uptake and insulin signaling.

claim: Increased glucose production was observed in AdHk2KO mice under hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp conditions.
source: We indeed observed increased glucose production in AdHk2KO mice under hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp conditions (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by clamp study data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: AdHk2KO mice displayed significantly higher production of glucose upon pyruvate injection compared to controls.
source: AdHk2KO mice displayed significantly higher production of glucose upon pyruvate injection, compared to controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by PTT data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Gluconeogenic genes (G6pc and Pepck) were upregulated in AdHk2KO liver.
source: Consistent with the observed increase in pyruvate-dependent glucose production, gluconeogenic genes (G6pc and Pepck) were upregulated in AdHk2KO liver (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Enhanced hepatic glucose production accounts for the severity of glucose intolerance in AdHk2KO mice.
source: These findings suggest that enhanced hepatic glucose production accounts for the severity of glucose intolerance in AdHk2KO mice.
evidence: Based on inference from glucose production and gene expression data.

claim: Loss of adipose HK2 non-cell-autonomously promotes glucose intolerance by enhancing hepatic glucose production.
source: Thus, loss of adipose HK2 non-cell-autonomously promotes glucose intolerance by enhancing hepatic glucose production.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing increased hepatic glucose production in AdHk2KO mice.

claim: Expression of Srebp1c, Mlxipl/Chrebp, and fatty acid synthesis genes was maintained or mildly increased in liver of AdHk2KO mice.
source: Expression of Srebp1c, Mlxipl/Chrebp, and fatty acid synthesis genes (Acly, Scd1, Fasn, and Acc) was maintained, even mildly increased, in liver of AdHk2KO mice (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: FASN and ACC protein levels were slightly increased in liver of AdHk2KO mice.
source: FASN and ACC protein levels were also slightly increased in liver of AdHk2KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Loss of adipose HK2 does not inhibit hepatic lipogenesis although hepatic glucose production is enhanced.
source: These findings indicate that loss of adipose HK2 does not inhibit hepatic lipogenesis although hepatic glucose production is enhanced.
evidence: Based on inference from gene and protein expression data.

claim: The increased hepatic glucose production and maintained lipogenesis in AdHk2KO mice resembles selective insulin resistance observed in diabetic patients.
source: The increased hepatic glucose production and maintained lipogenesis, as observed in AdHk2KO mice, resembles a condition in diabetic patients known as selective insulin resistance (Brown and Goldstein, 2008; see below).
evidence: Based on inference comparing mouse phenotype to human condition, with citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of adipose HK2 causes selective insulin resistance and thereby contributes to the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes.
source: Thus, loss of adipose HK2 causes selective insulin resistance and thereby contributes to the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings and comparison to diabetic phenotype.

claim: Hepatic triglyceride levels were unchanged in AdHk2KO mice despite increased expression of lipogenic genes and enzymes in liver.
source: We note that hepatic triglyceride (TG) levels were unchanged in AdHk2KO mice despite increased expression of lipogenic genes and enzymes in liver (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E) and increased de novo TG synthesis (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by TG measurement and lipogenesis assay data shown in Figure 5D, 5E, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: De novo-synthesized hepatic TG in AdHk2KO mice is likely secreted and delivered to adipose tissue for storage.
source: Most likely, de novo-synthesized hepatic TG in AdHk2KO mice is secreted and delivered to adipose tissue for storage, as suggested by the higher levels of circulating TG and cholesterol in AdHk2KO mice (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: Based on inference from plasma lipid measurements shown in Figure 5F-G.

claim: Adipose lipogenesis non-cell-autonomously inhibits hepatic glucose production.
source: Adipose lipogenesis non-cell-autonomously inhibits hepatic glucose production (Vijayakumar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Adipose-specific knockout of ChREBP decreases adipose lipogenesis and thereby increases hepatic glucose production.
source: Adipose-specific knockout of the transcription factor ChREBP decreases adipose lipogenesis and thereby increases hepatic glucose production (Ortega-Prieto and Postic, 2019; Vijayakumar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Glucose-derived metabolites promote ChREBP activity.
source: Glucose-derived metabolites have been shown to promote ChREBP activity (Dentin et al., 2012; Kabashima et al., 2003; Kawaguchi et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2016; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Expression of Mlxipl-beta/Chrebp-beta, but not Mlxipl-alpha/Chrebp-alpha, was significantly decreased in adipose tissue of AdHk2KO mice.
source: Expression of Mlxipl-beta/Chrebp-beta, but not Mlxipl-alpha/Chrebp-alpha, was significantly decreased in adipose tissue of AdHk2KO mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Lipogenic genes and enzymes were down-regulated in adipose tissue of AdHk2KO mice.
source: Consistent with reduced Mlxipl-beta/Chrebp-beta expression, lipogenic genes and enzymes and ultimately lipogenesis were down-regulated in adipose tissue of AdHk2KO mice (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR, immunoblotting, and lipogenesis assay data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Lipogenesis was down-regulated in adipose tissue of AdHk2KO mice.
source: Consistent with reduced Mlxipl-beta/Chrebp-beta expression, lipogenic genes and enzymes and ultimately lipogenesis were down-regulated in adipose tissue of AdHk2KO mice (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Supported by lipogenesis assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Loss of adipose HK2 causes loss of ChREBP activity and lipogenesis in adipose tissue.
source: The above findings indicate that loss of adipose HK2 causes loss of ChREBP activity and lipogenesis in adipose tissue.
evidence: Based on inference from gene expression and lipogenesis data.

claim: Loss of adipose HK2 promotes hepatic glucose production via loss of adipose lipogenesis.
source: Furthermore, our above findings combined with previous literature (Vijayakumar et al., 2017) suggest that loss of adipose HK2 promotes hepatic glucose production via loss of adipose lipogenesis.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings combined with published literature.

claim: Adipose tissue weight in AdHk2KO mice is essentially unchanged despite loss of lipogenesis, likely due to a compensating supply of TG from liver.
source: We note that adipose tissue weight in AdHk2KO mice is essentially unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) despite loss of lipogenesis, likely due to a compensating supply of TG from liver (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Based on inference from tissue weight and lipid measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and Figure 5D-F.

claim: Insulin inhibited isoproterenol-induced NEFA release in adipose tissue from control mice, but not in explants from AdHk2KO mice.
source: Ex vivo, insulin inhibited isoproterenol-induced NEFA release in adipose tissue from control mice, but not in explants from AdHk2KO mice (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by ex vivo NEFA release assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Glucose administration inhibited NEFA release only in control mice, not in AdHk2KO mice.
source: In vivo, glucose administration inhibited NEFA release only in control mice (Figure 6F–G) despite similar physiological increases insulin levels in fasted AdHk2KO and control mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), in agreement with the above ex vivo experiment.
evidence: Supported by in vivo NEFA measurement data shown in Figure 6F-G and insulin measurement shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of HK2 simultaneously inhibits lipogenesis and promotes NEFA release in adipose tissue, both of which contribute to de-repression of hepatic glucose production.
source: These findings suggest that loss of HK2 simultaneously inhibits lipogenesis and promotes NEFA release in adipose tissue, both of which contribute to de-repression of hepatic glucose production.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings on lipogenesis and NEFA release.

claim: HFD-fed mice exhibited decreased Hk2 mRNA in sWAT but not in vWAT or BAT.
source: HFD-fed mice exhibited decreased Hk2 mRNA in sWAT but not in vWAT or BAT (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: HK2 synthesis is down-regulated at the transcriptional level in sWAT, and at a post-transcriptional level in vWAT and BAT.
source: This suggests that HK2 synthesis is down-regulated at the transcriptional level in sWAT, and at a post-transcriptional level in vWAT and BAT.
evidence: Based on inference from mRNA and protein expression patterns.

claim: The amount of AHA-containing HK2 polypeptides was significantly decreased in vWAT explants from HFD-fed mice.
source: The amount of AHA-containing HK2 polypeptides was significantly decreased in vWAT explants from HFD-fed mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by AHA-incorporation proteomics data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: HFD down-regulates HK2 in vWAT by inhibiting Hk2 mRNA translation.
source: Thus, HFD down-regulates HK2 in vWAT by inhibiting Hk2 mRNA translation.
evidence: Based on inference from AHA-incorporation data showing reduced HK2 synthesis.

claim: Foxk1 and Foxk2 expression was significantly decreased in sWAT, but not in vWAT or BAT, of HFD-fed mice.
source: Foxk1 and Foxk2 expression was significantly decreased in sWAT, but not in vWAT or BAT, of HFD-fed mice (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 7C-E.

claim: HFD appears to down-regulate HK2 in sWAT by inhibiting FOXK1/2 and thereby expression of the Hk2 gene.
source: Thus, HFD appears to down-regulate HK2 in sWAT by inhibiting FOXK1/2 and, thereby, expression of the Hk2 gene.
evidence: Based on inference from FOXK1/2 expression data and published literature on FOXK regulation of Hk2.

claim: Loss of adipose HK2 is sufficient to cause glucose intolerance in two ways: reduced glucose disposal by adipose tissue and de-repressed glucose production in liver.
source: In this study, we show that HFD causes hyperglycemia by inducing loss of HK2 specifically in adipose tissue. Loss of adipose HK2 is sufficient to cause glucose intolerance, in two ways (Figure 8).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings, with reference to Figure 8.

claim: HK2 loss results in reduced glucose disposal by adipose tissue due to the inability of adipocytes to trap and metabolize non-phosphorylated glucose.
source: First, HK2 loss results in reduced glucose disposal by adipose tissue due to the inability of adipocytes to trap and metabolize non-phosphorylated glucose (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on inference from glucose uptake data shown in Figure 5A and established knowledge of HK2 function.

claim: Loss of adipose HK2 is a mechanism of diet-induced insulin insensitivity and hyperglycemia.
source: We propose that loss of adipose HK2 is a mechanism of diet-induced insulin insensitivity and hyperglycemia.
evidence: Based on inference from all experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: In liver, insulin normally represses glucose production to decrease blood glucose and up-regulates lipogenesis to increase energy storage.
source: In liver, insulin normally represses glucose production to decrease blood glucose and up-regulates lipogenesis to increase energy storage.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of insulin action in liver.

claim: In type 2 diabetes, insulin fails to inhibit glucose production yet stimulates lipogenesis, hence the liver is selectively insulin resistant.
source: Paradoxically, in type 2 diabetes, insulin fails to inhibit glucose production yet stimulates lipogenesis, hence the liver is selectively insulin resistant (Brown and Goldstein, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Selective insulin resistance occurs despite intact hepatic insulin signaling.
source: Furthermore, previous findings suggest that selective insulin resistance occurs despite intact hepatic insulin signaling (Titchenell et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Loss of adipose HK2 causes selective insulin resistance without affecting hepatic insulin signaling.
source: Consistent with these previous findings, we observed that loss of adipose HK2 causes selective insulin resistance without affecting hepatic insulin signaling.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing maintained hepatic insulin signaling in AdHk2KO mice.

claim: Loss of adipose HK2 is a mechanism for selective insulin resistance in liver and ultimately diabetes.
source: Thus, we propose that loss of adipose HK2 is a mechanism for selective insulin resistance in liver and ultimately diabetes.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings and comparison to diabetic phenotype.

claim: Decreased lipogenesis and increased NEFA release in adipose tissue, due to loss of HK2, may promote glucose production.
source: As described above, one possible explanation is that decreased lipogenesis and increased NEFA release in adipose tissue, due to loss of HK2, promotes glucose production (Figure 6; Perry et al., 2015; Titchenell et al., 2016; Vijayakumar et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings and citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of adipose HK2 may cause increased hepatic glucose production via the central nervous system.
source: Another interesting possibility is that loss of adipose HK2 causes increased hepatic glucose production via the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: Based on speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Adipose tissue has a sensory nervous system which may communicate with the liver via the sympathetic nervous system.
source: Adipose tissue has a sensory nervous system (Blaszkiewicz et al., 2019; Fishman and Dark, 1987; Frei et al., 2022; Kreier et al., 2006; Makwana et al., 2021; Song et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2022) which may communicate with the liver via the sympathetic nervous system.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and speculation about potential communication pathways.

claim: Sympathetic activity promotes hepatic glucose production.
source: Sympathetic activity promotes hepatic glucose production (Niijima and Fukuda, 1973; Shimazu and Fukuda, 1965).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Increased glucose uptake by the liver due to reduced glucose disposal in adipose tissue may stimulate hepatic glucose production.
source: A third possibility to explain increased hepatic glucose production is that increased glucose uptake by the liver due to reduced glucose disposal in adipose tissue may stimulate hepatic glucose production, consistent with the demonstration by Kim et al. that hepatic ChREBP promotes glucose production (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on speculation with citation to published literature.

claim: The phenotype of AdHk2KO mice is similar to that of adipose-specific GLUT4 knockout mice.
source: The phenotype of AdHk2KO mice is similar to that of adipose-specific GLUT4 knockout mice (Abel et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on comparison with published literature.

claim: Both GLUT4 and HK2 knockout mice display reduced lipogenesis in adipose tissue and are hyperglycemic due to decreased glucose disposal in adipose tissue and increased glucose production in the liver.
source: Both knockout mice display reduced lipogenesis in adipose tissue and are hyperglycemic due to decreased glucose disposal in adipose tissue and increased glucose production in the liver (Vijayakumar et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on comparison with published literature.

claim: HFD prevents ChREBP activation and lipogenesis in adipose tissue independently of GLUT4 expression.
source: Importantly, one of these studies showed that HFD inhibits ChREBP activity in adipose tissue independently of GLUT4 expression (Herman et al., 2012), concluding that the underlying mechanism of HFD-induced inhibition of ChREBP and hyperglycemia is still unknown.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The physiological mechanism of HFD-induced inhibition of adipose ChREBP and lipogenesis, and consequently hyperglycemia, may be loss of HK2.
source: Our findings suggest that the physiological mechanism of HFD-induced inhibition of adipose ChREBP and lipogenesis, and consequently hyperglycemia, may be loss of HK2.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings.

claim: The primary defect in adipose tissue of HFD-fed mice is not at the level of GLUT4 expression and glucose transport, but rather at the level of HK2 expression and glucose phosphorylation.
source: Thus, we propose that the primary defect in adipose tissue of HFD-fed mice is not at the level of GLUT4 expression and glucose transport, but rather at the level of HK2 expression and glucose phosphorylation.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings showing early HK2 loss compared to GLUT4.

claim: Expression of glucokinase in adipose tissue has been shown to prevent insulin insensitivity in HFD-fed mice.
source: Importantly, expression of glucokinase (also known as HK4, hepatic hexokinase) in adipose tissue has been shown to prevent insulin insensitivity in HFD-fed mice (Muñoz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Global heterozygous Hk2 knockout mice have normal, even better, glucose tolerance compared to controls.
source: A previous study demonstrated that global heterozygous Hk2 knockout mice have normal, even better, glucose tolerance compared to controls (Heikkinen et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Global GLUT4 knockout mice are glucose tolerant due to a compensatory increase in glucose uptake in liver.
source: We note that adipose-specific GLUT4 knockout mice display glucose intolerance (Abel et al., 2001), but global GLUT4 knockout mice are glucose tolerant due to a compensatory increase in glucose uptake in liver (Katz et al., 1995; Ranalletta et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Global ablation of HK2 mice may provoke a compensatory response to maintain systemic glucose homeostasis.
source: Global ablation of HK2 mice may provoke an even stronger compensatory response to maintain systemic glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential compensatory mechanisms.

claim: Adipose-specific Rab10 knockout mice display reduced GLUT4 translocation and ~50% reduction in insulin-stimulated glucose disposal in isolated adipocytes.
source: A previous study showed that adipose-specific Rab10 knockout mice display reduced GLUT4 translocation to the plasma membrane and thus a ~50% reduction in insulin-stimulated glucose disposal, in isolated adipocytes (Vazirani et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Adipose-specific Rab10 knockout mice failed to suppress hepatic glucose production and were insulin insensitive.
source: Importantly, adipose-specific Rab10 knockout mice failed to suppress hepatic glucose production and were thus insulin insensitive, indicating that a limited disruption in glucose metabolism in adipose tissue can significantly impact systemic insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A limited disruption in glucose metabolism in adipose tissue can significantly impact systemic insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis.
source: Importantly, adipose-specific Rab10 knockout mice failed to suppress hepatic glucose production and were thus insulin insensitive, indicating that a limited disruption in glucose metabolism in adipose tissue can significantly impact systemic insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Based on inference from published findings on Rab10 knockout mice.

claim: The partial loss of HK2 observed in obese mice and patients may be sufficient to impact systemic insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis.
source: Thus, the partial loss of HK2 observed in obese mice and patients may be sufficient to impact systemic insulin sensitivity and thereby glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental findings and comparison to published literature.

claim: An HK2-R42H mutation was found in naturally hyperglycemic Mexican cavefish.
source: We found an HK2-R42H mutation in naturally hyperglycemic Mexican cavefish.
evidence: Supported by DNA sequencing data.

claim: No human monogenic disease has been reported associated with mutations in the HK2 gene to date.
source: To date, no human monogenic disease has been reported associated with mutations in the HK2 gene.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge from literature review.

claim: 12 R42W and 4 R42Q alleles are reported in the genomAD database.
source: However, 12 R42W and 4 R42Q alleles are reported in the genomAD database (Karczewski et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to genomAD database.

claim: HK2 phosphorylates glucose to generate glucose-6-phosphate (G6P), the rate-limiting step in glycolysis, in an insulin-stimulated manner.
source: HK2 phosphorylates glucose to generate glucose-6-phosphate (G6P), the rate-limiting step in glycolysis, in an insulin-stimulated manner.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge of HK2 function.

claim: The insulin-stimulated transcription factors SREBP1c and ChREBP activate fatty acid synthesis genes and thereby promote de novo lipogenesis in liver.
source: The insulin-stimulated transcription factors sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 c (SREBP1c) and carbohydrate responsive element binding protein (ChREBP) activate fatty acid synthesis genes and thereby promote de novo lipogenesis in liver (Horton et al., 2002; Iizuka et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ChREBP has two isoforms: constitutively expressed ChREBPα promotes transcription of ChREBPβ which then activates lipogenic genes.
source: ChREBP has two isoforms. Constitutively expressed ChREBPα promotes transcription of ChREBPβ which then activates lipogenic genes (Herman et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: NEFA released from adipose tissue promotes glucose production in liver.
source: Non-esterified fatty acid (NEFA) released from adipose tissue, in addition to loss of adipose lipogenesis, promotes glucose production in liver (Perry et al., 2015; Titchenell et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ChREBP in adipose tissue both promotes lipogenesis and inhibits NEFA release.
source: Furthermore, ChREBP in adipose tissue both promotes lipogenesis and inhibits NEFA release (Vijayakumar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: FOXK1 and FOXK2 promote Hk2 transcription in adipose tissue.
source: It was recently reported that the forkhead transcription factors FOXK1 and FOXK2 promote Hk2 transcription in adipose tissue (Sukonina et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.
